implementation_notes: Swift's actor type absorbs the pattern into the language: the compiler enforces that actor-isolated state is accessed serially through the actor's executor, calls from outside are implicitly async, and await delivers the result - the Future role - so no proxy, activation queue or scheduler loop is written at all. What is not provided is a dedicated thread: isolation is by serialized executor, and suspension points allow reentrancy, so invariants spanning awaits need care. Fall back to the classic structure only on pre-5.5 toolchains or when a real dedicated thread is required.
pitfalls: Actor reentrancy: an actor function that awaits can interleave with other queued work, so re-check state after every suspension point.
Non-Sendable values cannot cross the actor boundary under strict concurrency checking; keep state inside and exchange value types.
Every actor call is asynchronous: one long synchronous computation inside the actor stalls all of its messages.

variants.name: Serial DispatchQueue + completion handlers (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: Before actors, the idiomatic realization was a serial DispatchQueue owning the object's state: the proxy dispatches each method body with queue.async, which serializes execution exactly like an activation queue, and results are delivered through completion handlers or a promise wrapper because closures cannot be awaited. It remains the right choice when the queue is already the application's synchronization mechanism or the work must stay off the cooperative thread pool.
pitfalls: Strong self capture inside q.async closures keeps the object alive and can form retain cycles; use [weak self] where the closure outlives the call.
Dispatching synchronously onto a queue from inside that same queue deadlocks (q.sync from q) - always know which queue you are on.
Completion-handler style spreads result handling: without a promise wrapper, errors are easily dropped and callers block to compensate.
